terms.meaning: The long food passage from the mouth to the anus.
Waves of contraction in the food pipe wall that push food down.
Tiny finger-like parts of the small intestine wall that increase the area for absorbing food.
A grass-eating animal that swallows food partly chewed, then brings it back to chew it thoroughly.
The muscular stomach chamber in birds, which grinds food with swallowed grit.
Tiny air sacs in the lungs where oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged.
The dome-shaped muscle under the chest that helps us to breathe.

items.name: Path of food
items.formula: Mouth → Oesophagus → Stomach → Small intestine → Large intestine → Rectum → Anus
items.example: Food passes through all of these in this order.

items.name: Saliva
items.example: Rice tastes sweet if you chew it for long.

items.name: Iodine test for starch
items.example: Boiled rice turns blue-black. Well-chewed rice hardly changes, because its starch has become sugar.

items.name: In the stomach
items.formula: Digestive juice breaks proteins. Acid kills bacteria. Mucus protects the stomach lining.
items.example: Without mucus, the stomach’s own acid would damage it.

items.name: Bile from the liver
items.formula: Mildly basic: it neutralises stomach acid and breaks fats into tiny droplets.
items.example: It makes an oily meal easier to digest.

items.name: Pancreatic juice
items.formula: Basic: it breaks down carbohydrates, proteins and fats.
items.example: The pancreas sends it to the small intestine.

items.name: Small intestine
items.formula: About 6 m long. Digestion finishes here and nutrients are absorbed.
items.example: It is the longest part of the alimentary canal.

items.name: Large intestine
items.formula: About 1.5 m long. It absorbs most of the remaining water and some salts.
items.example: What is left is stored in the rectum and passed out through the anus.

items.name: Celiac disease
items.formula: The body reacts badly to gluten, a protein in wheat, barley and rye.
items.example: Millets such as ragi and jowar have no gluten.

items.name: Path of air
items.formula: Nostrils → Windpipe → Two branches → Lungs → Alveoli
items.example: Hair and mucus in the nose trap dust, so breathe through the nose.

items.name: Breathing in
items.formula: Ribs go up and out, the diaphragm moves down, and the chest space grows.
items.example: Air is drawn into the lungs.

items.name: Breathing out
items.formula: Ribs go down and in, the diaphragm moves up, and the chest space shrinks.
items.example: Air is pushed out of the lungs.

items.name: Air we breathe in and out
items.formula: In: about 21% oxygen and 0.04% carbon dioxide. Out: about 16 to 17% oxygen and 4 to 5% carbon dioxide.
items.example: Your breath turns lime water milky, and room air from a syringe does not.

items.name: Respiration in cells
items.formula: Glucose + Oxygen → Carbon dioxide + Water + Energy
items.example: This is how nutrients become usable energy.

items.name: Circulatory system
items.formula: The heart pumps blood through blood vessels, carrying oxygen and nutrients and removing waste.
items.example: Blood brings oxygen from the lungs to every cell.

items.name: How a cow digests
items.formula: Grass goes to the rumen and is partly digested. The cud returns to the mouth to be chewed again.
items.example: This is called rumination, and it is why a resting cow keeps chewing.

items.name: Fish
items.formula: Breathe through gills, taking oxygen dissolved in water.

items.name: Adult frog
items.formula: Lungs on land, moist skin in water.
items.example: A tadpole has gills, but it loses them as it grows.

items.name: Earthworm
items.example: It has no lungs or gills.

mistakes.text: Breathing and respiration are different. Breathing is physical movement of air, and respiration is a chemical process in cells.
Exhaled air still has plenty of oxygen, about 16 to 17%. It is not all carbon dioxide.
The small intestine is the longer one. "Small" and "large" describe its width, since the large intestine is wider.
When you breathe in, the diaphragm moves down, not up.
